speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Immigration Act (IA) regulates residents and visitors’ entry into Singapore, their stay here, and exit from Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The last major amendment to IA was in 2012.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since then, the security threat has heightened significantly, including at our checkpoints, which are, unfortunately, attractive targets for terrorists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The checkpoints are also our first line of defence against terrorist threats, which emanate from outside Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In March 2016, a suicide bombing at Brussels Airport killed 17 persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just three months later, gunmen armed also with explosive belts, attacked Ataturk Airport in Istanbul, killing 45 persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Checkpoint operations have thus become increasingly complex and challenging.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To enhance border security and optimise Home Team resources deployed at the checkpoints, the Integrated Checkpoints Command (ICC) was introduced in 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICC strengthens coordination among Home Team departments by putting them under a unified command at the respective checkpoints, that is, all Home Team officers working at the checkpoints report to the same Commander.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This arrangement facilitates joint operations at the checkpoints, communications and information sharing and allows synergies to be reaped.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To enhance the Home Team's operational effectiveness at the checkpoints, Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officers will play a bigger role to support Police Officers to provide protective security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will enable the Home Team to more effectively prevent security incidents at the checkpoints and respond more swiftly when they do occur.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To achieve this, we need to expand the range of powers available to ICA officers to discharge their duties effectively at the checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Authorised Areas, as defined in the IA, generally refer to the air, land, and sea checkpoints in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include Changi and Seletar Airports, Woodlands and Tuas Checkpoints, Singapore Cruise Centre and the Marina Bay Cruise Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, ICA officers mainly rely on existing powers under the IA and Customs Act to conduct searches of vehicles, trains, vessels or persons, examine individuals, seize evidence and arrest persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Police Officers, on the other hand, are empowered to conduct searches on an individual only if the person has been arrested, or if there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the person has committed certain offences where the laws specifically allow for searches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include possession of arms and explosives, possession of an instrument likely to cause hurt and possession of controlled substances or evidence of drug offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, existing powers are not sufficient to protect the checkpoints in today’s security climate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, ICA officers are not able to search a person suspected of carrying an offensive weapon if he or she is not in the authorised area but is instead in public areas of Changi Airport, or at the bus stop outside Woodlands Checkpoint.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To be more effective, the powers have to be expanded so that ICA officers can intervene in any suspected security incident within or in the vicinity of the checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the ground, this will allow any ICA officer nearest to a security incident at the checkpoints to be the first responder.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Furthermore, ICA and Police Officers need to have wider powers of search to intervene more decisively to deal with criminal and security incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Police Officers today are not empowered to search suspected vandals even if surveillance cameras or other security sensors at the checkpoints have been damaged; the suspect must first be arrested before he can be searched.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is necessary for an ICA and Police Officer, whoever is nearest to an incident at the checkpoints, to pre-emptively and more effectively detect and address criminal and security threats at the checkpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The other powers in clause 4 which will be extended to ICA officers operating within and in the vicinity of Authorised Areas are similar to existing powers accorded to Police Officers under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: ICA officers will be empowered to arrest the individual if he is reasonably suspected to have committed an arrestable offence under Singapore laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similar to what I have explained earlier, this will enable ICA officers to respond to any security threat without having to wait for the arrival of Police Officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For non-arrestable offences, ICA officers will only be able to arrest an individual if the person refuses to give his or her name and residential address, or if the person gives a name or residential address believed to be false or gives an overseas residential address.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is similar to section 65 of the CPC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Post-incident investigations, including the prosecution of the arrested persons in the Courts, will remain the Police’s responsibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now move on to clause 5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will allow ICA to screen transit passengers more effectively, to better detect travellers of interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, clause 5 amends section 55(1)(k) to increase the quantum of penalties that the Minister may prescribe for the breach of regulations under the IA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Both the National Registration Act (NRA) and IA govern the proper registration of persons in Singapore for identification and security purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, the maximum penalties that the Minister may prescribe for the breach of regulations under the IA are significantly lower than those under NRA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I support the evolution and stepping up of the ICA officers’ job description as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With the increasing numbers of people passing through all the points of entry and checkpoints in Singapore daily, we have to certainly ensure we are ever ready any time of the day, night or under any conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, can I understand the following a bit further?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What kind of enhanced training will these ICA frontline officers be provided with in order to empower them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will there be some form of psychological preparedness training, briefing and counselling that they would be put through as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: My concern is that Police Officers have been prepared for these types of work from the beginning of their career, but these ICA officers may not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, the need to prepare them well with relevant skills, mindset and manage their psychological states as well in anticipating any possible acts or challenges in any form.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Since 2015, the ICC brings in the various Home Team agencies operating at our checkpoints under one command, and this is good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on this a bit more for our understanding?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, I feel that this ties in very well with this Bill’s implementation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister explain how they will be synergistic in terms of Singapore’s preparedness as well, and how will it enhance our plan to ringfence our safety and security?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I would also like to understand further how the coordination between ICA officers and staff at all our entry points will happen and how it will be coordinated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How fast can information be shared and, in terms of action, how rapid can the execution be when facing certain crises?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the case of a planned multi-site entry point incident, how fast and how well can our information sharing and coordination be?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is important because this is the current trend that we are seeing in terms of terrorist attacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The enhanced security proposed in this Bill is taking us in the right direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But besides policy, technology and infrastructure, there is also the human element and the human factors for us to consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, therefore, the buy-in, commitment and collaboration from the staff involved are highly important as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the intent is to enable the Home Team to deal with security incidents at the checkpoints more promptly by having ICA officers perform protective security functions in support of Police Officers, I have some questions on the expansion of the role of ICA officers and how they are being prepared to take on these additional duties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is given that the ICA officers are empowered under this Bill to carry out search and seizure duties and arrest suspects for offences under any written law.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the ICC policy was launched in 2015 to achieve greater operational coordination and provide clearer lines of responsibility and command for the officers from ICA, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) working together at the checkpoints, for example, faster operational responses and more successful interceptions of persons and vehicles of interest.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With ICA officers taking on duties of the Police, how would this impact the lines of responsibility across the various elements of the Home Team in carrying out their work at our checkpoints?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, ICA officers are already dealing with large numbers of travellers daily while under expectations from travellers for timely clearance at checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would arrangements be made to ease ICA officers into their new duties so that the additional duties are not too onerous?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, a Direct-Entry Sergeant in ICA would have undergone a 16-week non-residential ICA Basic Course (Sergeant) at the Home Team Academy while a Direct-Entry Sergeant in the Police Force would have undergone six months of residential training, including lessons in criminal law, physical training, community policing, as well as leadership development.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Males are required to be Physical Employment Standard (PES) A or PES B1L1 in order to qualify as a Direct-Entry Sergeant in the Police Force whereas only a PES A or B grade is required for ICA officers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What measures are being taken to better prepare our ICA officers so that they are able to carry out their new functions under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, the starting salary range for a Direct-Entry Sergeant in ICA is lower than the starting salary range for a Direct-Entry Sergeant in the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would the salaries of ICA officers be adjusted to take into account the additional duties that they are expected to perform?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In order to perform their duties better in their expanded role, the ICA officers need to be well-trained in protective security, especially during emergency situations.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With the enhanced responsibilities comes the need for upskilling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As such, would the career path for ICA officers be similarly enhanced?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a review of their career progression?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it is commendable that the ICC would be better equipped to deal with any checkpoint incidents with minimal delay.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is essential to manage threats against Singapore, and citizens, too, would realise the importance of being vigilant against security threats.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, the joint responsibility of both authorities and our citizens to ensure and enforce stringent checks at the border.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, how can civilians play their part in identifying and reporting potential threats?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we better train them to be, by passing information that is relevant?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The collection of information of transit passengers is of significant importance for security and traceability.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How will the information be shared readily, responsively and constructively with the other agencies to circumvent threats and adverse incidents?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there cross-border collaborations to better optimise data use and information?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are the officers given sufficient training to help them better handle the expanded and enriched responsibilities?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On protection for the officers, are the officers better protected against complaints and legal actions from a suspect who may be injured as the officers restrain the suspect?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And so, how much and how well are the officers protected?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a consideration to enhance workplace insurance or workplace injury compensation for the officers with this enhancement of job responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are giving ICA officers more authority to perform security screenings, conduct search and seizure duties, as well as arrests, and I think it is a good move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the terrorism threat becoming more prevalent, police and security forces around the world are shouldering heavier responsibilities to protect the community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I feel ICA officers could be counted on to handle more responsibilities as befit their training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would, in turn, free up the Police for other responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my second question is in relation to investigation work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister enlighten the House on the training for an ICA officer compared to a Police Officer?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In regard to the enhanced powers for ICA officers, can the Minister also share plans to ensure that the officers have the prerequisite training to handle the enhanced powers and search authority that they have now with these changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This also includes the proper handling of individuals and suspects as part of the search but also taking into consideration the sensitivities and communication skills needed with the extra responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Border security, Mr Deputy Speaker, is of paramount importance, and it is certainly not the sole responsibility of ICA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More must be done to educate the masses and obtain everyone's support and cooperation, so that we can close any gaps in our security network.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should thus closely scrutinise the powers this Bill gives to ICA officers to ensure that there are sound bases and sufficient checks for an extension of power.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As was noted in the Ministry of Home Affairs' (MHA's) press release on the Bill, the intention of giving ICA officers such powers is to enable them to respond to incidents and contain situations before Police Officers arrive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The powers that are granted to ICA officers should be constrained insofar as they are necessary for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The language of section 51AA(6) and (7) is similar to section 22 of the CPC which allows the Police to take long statements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike section 23 of the CPC, the amendments do not expressly require persons being questioned to be given notice that choosing to remain silent may have a bad effect on their case in Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, is there a duty to inform the person being examined of their privilege against self-incrimination under section 51AA(6) and does the failure to inform the person of their right to remain silent affect the admissibility of the statement or the ability to draw adverse inferences from the statement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Laypersons may not know that they have such a right and it seems only fair that they should be informed of this right if the privilege against self-incrimination is to have any substance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to remain silent under section 51AA(5) would be very weak in practice if there is no need to inform an individual of their right to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is those who are ignorant of the law and the most vulnerable who would suffer the most.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, section 51AA(7) sets out requirements, which are intended to be procedural safeguards for the person's whose statement is taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the exercise of Police powers is governed by CPC and the Police General Orders (PGO) issued by the Commissioner of Police.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will rules or guidelines similar to PGO be issued for ICA officers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As highlighted earlier, these powers are only transitory in that they are intended for ICA officers to be able to contain the situation until the Police arrive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In line with the spirit of unifying the command and control structure that underlies the ICC concept, surely closer coordination between the Police and ICA officers could be expected in responding to these incidences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are three main facets of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is the expanded role of ICA officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second is the provision for the collecting of personal identifiers of transit passengers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And the third is the increased penalty for breach of regulations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The expanded role of ICA officers promotes synergy and collaboration of the ICC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Started in 2015, the ICC organises Singapore's borders into three domains: air, land and sea.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One domain head oversees operations of all Home Team officers in that domain, whether they be Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), Police or ICA officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was a further step to optimise the organisation of our Home Team resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Back in 2003, the ICA was born with the merging of Singapore Immigration and Registration and the Checkpoints Operations of Customs and Excise Department.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, this Bill seeks to confer certain Police's powers on ICA officers so that we are able to respond to situations promptly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This move in this Bill keeps our Home Team agencies nimble, flexible and able to address the changing needs in these changing times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This includes security screening under subsection (4) of the new proposed section 51AA under clause 4.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with pass to intervene to prevent a crime and to cordon off an area to preserve a crime scene under subsections (13) and (14), these powers allow for a prompt response and would aid with the investigation process of crimes committed near the border.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through prompter collection and preservation of evidence of an act at or near the crime scene, there may be more evidence and more cogent, reliable and accurate evidence collected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is hoped that this will greatly enhance the administration of justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, through the powers of arrest under clause 4 of section 51AA(8) to (10), ICA officers' presence at the borders will strengthen deterrence of the Home Team officers there.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The procedural safeguards are in subsections (11) and (12), with subsection (12) playing an important signal that the Police are still primarily in charge of these policing duties.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the ICA officers' powers are restricted to offences committed in the authorised area and its vicinity, an arrested person has to be ultimately handed over to the Police, the relationship between the ICA officers is clearly delineated for effective collaboration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than abrogating from the Police's primary duty, these expanded powers further promote prompt and effective responses to a situation at our borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even with a strong uniformed presence near the borders, there are some who still dare to commit offences in the area.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ICA officers will be equipped, through training, and they will not be hamstrung if they witness or have reason to believe that an offence is being committed before their very eyes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This supportive role will enhance the ICA's powers to protect Singapore and strengthen security at our borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second main feature of this Bill is the collection of personal identifiers from passengers transiting through our airport.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What has happened in some countries previously is that illegal immigrants travel using forged documents, staying in the airport lounge to connect to their next destination.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alternatively, illegal immigrants cleared immigration using genuine documents but switch to forged documents or even took other persons' boarding passes inside the travel lounge.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By collecting personal identifiers from those transiting through Singapore airport, it will be harder to commit identity fraud.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, there has been a proliferation of fraudulent documents that facilitate travel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not just boarding passes that can be faked.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lost passports and faked IDs have increased in number.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to a Political article, EU passport fraud epidemic, which refers to EU passport fraud epidemic in January this year, the number of lost and stolen documents in the EU has doubled in five years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are 250,000 stolen or lost Syrian and Iraqi passports, including blank documents, very easily utilised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A report by the University of East London entitled "Mining the dark web, drugs and fake IDs" showed that whilst counterfeit documents make up a smaller percentage of the market compared to drugs, they are readily available.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the January issue of S Rajaratnam's School of International Studies and titled "Counter terrorist trends and analyses", a small percentage of combat-hardened fighters use forged, adapted and fraudulently-obtained genuine documents to travel home to conduct attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The collection of personal identifiers of transit passengers is now more common in today's increasingly globalised world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such countries include New Zealand and the United Arab Emirates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, travellers who remain in the transit area do not need a visa.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a provision is necessary and timely to ensure security in our airports and it should be implemented with the utmost care to stringently secure the information collected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If such personalised data gets into the wrong hands, the cure may be worse than the ill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, through stringent and high-quality implementation, our position as a travel elite hub and Singapore airports' reputation will grow stronger by being more secure and lowering the possibility for identity fraud and a safer transit area.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to ensure that our security measures are tight and kept up to date or even ahead of the technologies used by criminals to manoeuvre their way around the proper safeguards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another feature of the Bill is the increased maximum penalty for breach of regulations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This update of the maximum penalty ensures that inflation does not rob the penalty of its punitive effect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Tuas and Woodlands checkpoints handle a high volume of people daily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We clearly need to future-proof our security coverage and provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With volume, potential perpetrators of harm seek vulnerabilities during busy periods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not merely a matter of volume.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The nature and essence of threats evolve quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Being at the frontline of security incidents, our ICA officers required powers to quickly intervene and resolve issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Empowering them with greater authority will boost the level of safety and security and be efficient.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This contrasts with the current situation where the information is obtained only from travellers at immigration counters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Transit passengers make up about a third of Changi Airport’s passengers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We cannot allow terrorists to use Changi as a transit stop.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we cannot allow this extra layer of checks to cause transit passengers to encounter delays in the process of transferring from one flight to another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What measures will be taken to ensure that inconveniences are minimised, even as security steps are being increased?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is new biometric technology used to handle the increasing load?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With increased responsibilities coming their way, we must also ensure that our officers are equal to the task.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The law is, after all, only as effective as the officers using them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They must be trained to enhance their knowledge, skills and capability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can SPF officers be involved in helping their ICA colleagues to take on the new powers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Interagency capabilities and operabilities are even more critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to ensure that our officers operate well together as one unit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Other than training on their “hard” skills that are directly related to their profession, are ICA and SPF officers provided with "softer skills”, such as cultural intelligence, as their job requires them to deal with people from different cultures and nationalities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Another aspect of manpower and human capital, security work cannot be easily substituted with technology and enhanced legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Experience and street knowledge are essential elements built up over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry must continue to leverage such strengths of our officers, especially when more powers are vested in them to meet our ever-evolving security threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This might require buttressing our competencies with experienced officers from SPF and other enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the above, the Bill is important to harden our borders without sacrificing on our efficacy and efficiency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They raised many useful points which I shall try to address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked for a further elaboration of the ICC concept, and how the Bill will enhance Singapore’s preparedness for emergencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how the Bill will impact the lines of responsibilities across the various Home Team agencies working at the checkpoints.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An ICA Domain Commander now helms all Home Team operations in each of the three domains.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we have a unified command structure under a single commander.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With this, the lines of responsibility as well as accountability are very clear and will help in ensuring that the security and operations in each domain are properly taken care of.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By doing so, we have also strengthened the coordination amongst the officers from the various Home Team departments deployed at the checkpoints because there is a unified command structure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another potential benefit of the ICC is in joint operations as compared to operations mounted separately by each Home Team Department.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, it did not take long for the benefit to be realised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The timely sharing of information and exchange of analyses made the critical difference.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The subjects were eventually repatriated to Batam and handed over to the Indonesian counter-terrorism unit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef also asked about the coordination among ICA officers at the various checkpoints, and how prepared we are for a planned multi-site incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Any terrorist incidents involving multiple checkpoints will be coordinated by the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Home Team has developed joint operation plans for such scenarios and we have been exercising them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And some of these exercises were publicised earlier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Exercise Quicksilver, which is a series of regular internal exercises, involves scenarios of multiple attacks at the land and sea domains where officers are not notified beforehand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, it is a surprise exercise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of these surprise exercises was held in October 2016 and it involved more than 3,000 officers across the Home Team and SAF.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The aim of these exercises is, of course, to prepare ourselves to respond to security incidents as soon as possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I should stress that it is not just speed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is also the quality and the effectiveness of the response that matter.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And that is why we are making these amendments to ensure that, when we respond, the response is an effective one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All Members who have spoken felt it was important for the ICA officers to be properly trained to exercise the enhanced powers, and I fully agree.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Before I outline our training approach, let me clarify what is expected of the ICA officers under this Bill, something that Mr Christopher de Souza had also talked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ICA officers are not expected to become Police Officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What this Bill seeks to do is to empower ICA officers, who are usually the majority at the checkpoints, to respond to security incidents within and in the vicinity of the checkpoint.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will further enhance the ICC concept, where the nearest Home Team officers to a security incident at the checkpoint will be the first responders acting swiftly to mitigate the situation instead of waiting for the Police Officers to arrive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Once the Police Officers arrive at the scene, there is a clear understanding that they will take over management and investigation of the incident, including the recording of statements from arrested persons and working with the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) to prosecute the person in Court.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The training for ICA officers is, therefore, designed specifically for them to be the first responder rather than full-fledged Police Officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With this consideration in mind, ICA has been working with SPF to develop appropriate training courses for ICA officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We need courses for newly appointed as well as current serving officers who are selected to perform protective security functions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are modules on the legislative provisions, management of protective security incidents, interview skills and search techniques.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Classroom training is also complemented by on-the-job training with Police Officers serving as coaches, a point which addresses Mr Desmond Choo’s observation that the Police Officers have much that they can share to help ICA colleagues get up to speed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, ICA officers will join Police Officers for relevant protective security training courses, such as the Public Security First Responder Training, where officers are given tactical movement training to augment their existing competencies in firearms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: ICA officers will be assessed to a similar standard as Police Officers in these areas before they are deployed for protective security duties.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All new ICA officers will also undergo the ICC training to equip them to operate effectively at the ICC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is something Mr Louis Ng asked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef also asked if ICA officers will be prepared psychologically for their enhanced roles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During their basic training, ICA recruits already undergo psychological training to boost their resilience and prepare them for the challenges in their work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Frontline supervisors are trained on how to look out for distressed officers and to provide support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, selected ICA officers are trained as para-counsellors to look out for and support their fellow colleagues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The officers are further supported by the ICA Psychological Services Branch, which provides staff counselling services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As part of the ICC training programmes, ICA officers will be exposed to challenging situations that they may face in the course of duty and trained on how they can respond to such circumstances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These range from managing security incidents, such as travellers attempting to dash through without immigration clearance, to dealing with possible bomb threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scenario-based trainings, along with on-the-job training with Police Officers, will help to prepare ICA officers for their new roles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if ICA officers and Police Officers are provided with training on soft skills, in particular on cultural intelligence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As part of their training, ICA and SPF officers learn how to manage members of the public in a professional and tactful manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Officers are trained to be mindful and sensitive towards cultural differences when interacting with members of the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is reinforced through in-service training and reminders on the job.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The very nature of ICA's work at the checkpoints involves interactions with people from all nationalities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our officers have generally done well, with our security-focused, service-conscious approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: ICA officers deployed at Changi Airport also undergo a programme to further equip them with skills to deliver to be part of the "Changi Experience" for travellers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To be clear, the intent is to minimise the time ICA officers will detain an individual before handing him over to Police Officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why the new section 51AA(12)(a) in clause 4 requires the ICA officer to immediately inform a Police Officer of the arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, there may be instances where the Police need more time to take over custody of the person, such as during major emergencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat has asked whether it was necessary for the ICA officer to hand over an accused to the Police immediately, and if ICA officers can perform the required investigations instead, to free up Police resources.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have explained earlier, the intention is not for ICA officers to take over the Police's duties, and Police Officers are still best placed to carry out the post-incident investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about the need for safeguards when ICA officers take statements under the new section 51AA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He pointed out that the provisions of section 51AA(6) and (7) were similar to section 22 of the CPC but unlike section 23 of the CPC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for section 23 of the CPC, the statement is recorded from an individual after he or she has been charged with an offence and will be prosecuted in Court.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there are material differences between the two types of statements provided for under the different sections of the CPC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The intent behind providing ICA officers with the powers of examination under the new section 51AA of the Bill is to allow ICA officers to conduct preliminary fact-finding and checks during or immediately after an incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to the admissibility of such statements, existing case laws interpreting section 22 of the CPC will similarly apply and be followed by the Courts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If I may reiterate, post-incident investigations, including the recording of statements under section 23 of the CPC and prosecution of individuals in Court, remain the responsibilities of the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After ICA officers hand over the accused person to the Police, the investigation processes, as well as the safeguards, will be no different from today’s processes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked what it means for ICA officers to use reasonable force within the new section 51AA(10)(b) to make an arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The usage of the term "reasonable" can also be found in section 75 of the CPC, which is applicable to Police Officers and from which this new section is adapted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, officers should not use firearms to shoot an unarmed person who may be trying to evade arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have explained earlier, ICA officers will be trained to use their enhanced powers appropriately which, of course, include the proper use of force.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if the salaries of ICA officers will be adjusted to take into account the additional duties that they are expected to perform.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi also asked if the career progression for ICA officers will be enhanced.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I assure Mr Patrick Tay that it is in our interest to assess these factors holistically and whether any expansion of duties or work conditions warrant adjustments, so that the officers are reasonably remunerated, whatever the roles they perform and we continue to be able to retain them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, the career progression paths for ICA officers are regularly reviewed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to keep these schemes of service updated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if ICA officers will be better protected against complaints and legal actions from suspects who had been restrained by ICA officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are existing mechanisms within the Home Team departments to investigate complaints or allegations of misconduct, and officers are empowered to carry out their duties without fear as long as they act in good faith and in accordance with established protocols.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where insurance is concerned, ICA officers enjoy the same coverage as all other Home Team officers, such as the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All officers who sustain injuries during the course of work will have their medical expenses fully covered when they receive treatment at Government or restructured hospitals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about the importance of transit passenger screening and emphasised the need to handle data collected with care.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked how data collected from the screening will be shared and if there are cross-border collaborations to optimise data use and information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Transit passengers are currently not required to present themselves for immigration clearance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The screening of transit passengers will thus allow ICA to detect travellers of interest or those who may be using stolen or lost passports.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why we need the personal identifiers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are existing provisions in the IA that enable the sharing of such information with law enforcement agencies and other agencies for the purposes of investigation and for the prevention and detection of threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there are also strict protocols governing the sharing of information and safekeeping of data, and they will continue to apply.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked what measures will be taken to ensure that inconveniences to transit passengers can be minimised even as we step up security measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In introducing transit security screening, MHA and ICA work closely with the Ministry of Transport (MOT), CAAS and CAG, as well as airlines, to minimise the impact on passengers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We conducted field trials to test the procedures and those resulted in several process refinements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we now assess that the minimum connecting times that can be maintained for most of the instances will remain unchanged.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are also working with CAG on protocols to clear passengers with very short connecting times.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked how members of the public can also play their part to identify and report potential or possible threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I really want to thank her for raising this very important point about citizens' active participation because that can be the crucial difference in ensuring Singapore’s security.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We started the SGSecure movement in 2016 precisely to raise public awareness of the threats we face and to increase their level of preparedness in the event of a terror attack in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members of the public can certainly play their part in identifying potential threats in their neighbourhood or surroundings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the checkpoints, they should not hesitate to inform the ICA officers and the Police if they come across anything suspicious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members of the public can also report suspicious activities to the authorities via the SGSecure app, and I am glad to say that we regularly get such alerts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the support of this House, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.
